People slid out of apartments like coins being tossed from a fountain, each one landing with a soft clunk on the pavement below. Some wore worn-out sneakers, while others had on gleaming high heels that turned their entire bodies into urban landscapes. All of them looked up, stretched their arms and kindled a fire in their hearts, the lights of the city encapsulating them like a warm hug.

Inside La Morella Café, a petite woman with unruly brown hair toiled in the kitchen, rinsing cups and stacking them with a methodical rhythm. Lena wore a faded apron that had been altered so many times, its seams seemed to have developed their own unique identity. She moved swiftly, slicing lemons like they were spaghetti threads from a narrator's grand-to-be-tale. As she worked, rays of sunlight wheeling through the window stirred watery patterns in the oilcloth coat she loved, miraculous masterpieces reminding her of life lived til the ink dries.

Lena was conditioned by exposure. Her neighborhood had mannerisms that comprised exhaustion, overcast skies giving birth to tense whispers of brand anticipation.
